To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the power density of a given energy source can vary by up to two orders of magnitude, depending on the location and orientation of the device, (ii) the power densities of different energy sources vary by more than three orders of magnitude, and (iii) the power densities achievable from different energy harvesting technologies also vary by more than two orders of magnitude.

(1) the most promising energy harvesting sources for sensor networks are solar, vibration, thermal and RF energy; (2) the most suitable energy conversion devices are thermoelectric, piezoelectric, electromagnetic and photovoltaic; (3) the most suitable power management devices are super capacitors and rechargeable batteries.
the most suitable power sources are solar and thermal, while the most suitable energy conversion mechanisms are thermopile and photovoltaic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel energy harvesting system for wireless sensor networks.
the design and implementation of wireless sensor networks (WSN) that harvest energy from the environment and use that energy to power the WSN.
the development and evaluation of energy harvesting systems for wireless sensor networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the energy harvesting technologies are not yet mature enough to be considered as the sole source of power supply for a WSN.
the energy harvesting technology for WSN is still in its early stages, but it is likely to become a reality in the future.
the energy harvesting technologies available today do not provide enough energy to power a wireless sensor node.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most promising energy sources for WSNs are vibration, thermal, and solar.
energy scavenging from the environment is a promising approach for the power supply of sensor networks, but the power available from most sources is too low to be useful for most sensor nodes.
the energy density of the energy source is the most important parameter for the energy harvesting system design and selection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
energy harvesting is a viable option for many sensor nodes.
the power density of a source is a poor indicator of its suitability for energy harvesting.
the most promising energy sources for WSNs are vibration, wind, and solar.
